title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, Fatouros IG, Kyparos A, Nikolaidis MG, Paschalis V
journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
population: 48 young men; four independent groups did a second identical bout of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks after the first
findings: Forty-eight young men performed two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions at 60 degrees per second); four independent groups performed the second bout 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks after the first. The abstract does not say how participants were assigned to the groups or how many were in each.

Isometric torque, range of motion, delayed-onset muscle soreness, muscle thickness, echo intensity, creatine kinase and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein were assessed before and 2 and 4 days after each bout.
The repeated-bout effect was evident at 3 and 6 weeks across most outcomes and remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers.
At 12 weeks no significant differences between bouts were observed at day 2 or day 4 for any outcome.

Exploratory equivalence analyses indicated that the effect was no longer meaningfully present at 12 weeks for isometric torque, range of motion, soreness, muscle thickness and echo intensity; the findings for creatine kinase and C-reactive protein remained inconclusive.
The authors conclude that the effect may persist for some outcomes for up to 9 weeks, and that by 12 weeks no meaningful effect was detectable at the time points assessed.
limitations: Isolated maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise in a laboratory, not running or downhill running. Young men only. Four independent groups, one second bout per group; the abstract states no group sizes and no randomisation, and the equivalence analyses are called exploratory. Abstract read on Europe PMC; the full text was not read.
implications: For this eccentric knee-extensor task, protection after one bout lasted at least 6 weeks for most outcomes and was gone by 12. That ends the statement that protection beyond 3 weeks is untested, but only for a lab task: no running study tests an interval beyond 3 weeks.

The first exposure of a downhill block need not be repeated every 3 weeks to keep protection for several weeks, and a first exposure much more than 9 to 12 weeks before heavy downhill work may have worn off. Both are extrapolations from a lab task to running.
